intros.market: The WebPKI certificate market is highly concentrated, with the top 5 CAs controlling 92.4% of issuance. Internet Security Research Group leads with 39.2% market share, followed by Google Trust Services at 20.9% and DigiCert at 15.3%. The HHI of 2370 indicates a moderately concentrated market, while 75 long-tail CAs collectively serve the remaining 7.6% of demand across 89 total trusted certificate authorities.
intros.trust: The four major root stores collectively trust 335 roots from 89 CA owners, but they disagree substantially on which roots to include. Only 90 roots appear in all four stores, while 142 roots exist exclusively in Microsoft's store and are absent from Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple. Just 38 CA owners have achieved inclusion across all four programs, creating operational complexity where certificate chains trusted in one browser environment may fail validation in another.
intros.conc: Three CAs control 75.5% of all publicly trusted certificates, creating systemic dependency on Internet Security Research Group, Google Trust Services, and DigiCert. The HHI of 2370 and CR3 concentration rate reflect a market structure where failure or compromise of any top-tier provider would immediately affect three-quarters of the encrypted web. This concentration sits alongside 75 long-tail CAs that collectively issue fewer than 8% of certificates but retain full trust store inclusion.
intros.tail: Seventy-five CAs operate with minimal issuance volume yet maintain full inclusion in major trust stores, each serving a fraction of the remaining 7.6% market share outside the top five providers. These low-volume operators face the same regulatory obligations and audit requirements as high-volume CAs but lack the operational scale and automation maturity of providers like Let's Encrypt or Google. The incident data shows that 54 CAs have been involved in the 1,567 recorded incidents, indicating that tail risk is not merely theoretical.
intros.geo: Certificate authority incorporation concentrates heavily in the United States, where 15 CAs account for 91.95% of global issuance. Europe hosts 44 CAs but commands only 7.96% of issuance, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively represent 0.09% despite serving regions with billions of internet users. This geographic imbalance means the WebPKI's operational resilience depends overwhelmingly on US-incorporated entities, separate from the legal jurisdiction risks those entities face.
intros.gov: Thirty government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but account for only 0.07% of issuance volume. These entities span regions including China, Russia, and various European nations, maintaining the technical capability to issue trusted certificates for any domain despite minimal current deployment. Their presence in root stores creates a trust surface disconnected from market activity, as their low issuance share does not reduce their ability to participate in the WebPKI.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk due to legal frameworks enabling compelled disclosure, surveillance, or extra-territorial authority: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey are designated moderate-risk based on evolving legal postures toward encryption and data sovereignty. CAs incorporated in these jurisdictions face legal obligations that may conflict with WebPKI governance expectations, regardless of their current issuance volume or operational practices.
intros.ops: CAs have reported 1,567 incidents across 54 certificate authorities, with misissuance leading at 610 events, followed by 504 governance failures and 330 revocation issues. Only 26% of incidents are self-detected, while root programs identify just 4%, automated tools 17%, and external researchers 18%, with audits contributing 8%. Policy failures account for 194 incidents and disclosure failures for 139, indicating that compliance breakdowns extend beyond technical misissuance to include governance and transparency obligations.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture varies across the 335 trusted roots, with algorithm and key size choices reflecting both legacy compatibility requirements and modern security standards. The trust surface includes roots still using 2048-bit RSA keys alongside those that have migrated to stronger parameters, creating a mixed cryptographic baseline across the ecosystem. This diversity reflects the slow rotation cycle of root certificates, which typically remain trusted for decades and must balance backward compatibility against evolving cryptographic threats.
intros.distrust: Sixteen distrust events have occurred across the documented history, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures and 10 following patterns of repeated issues. The posture distribution shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance, 3 of demonstrated incompetence, 3 of willful circumvention, 2 of argumentative noncompliance, and 1 accidental failure. The median runway from distrust announcement to removal is 1,185 days, reflecting both the operational complexity of trust store removal and the reluctance of root programs to create widespread certificate validation failures.
intros.policy: Of the 37 active TLS CAs measured for certificate validity behavior, 3 remain at risk of non-compliance with the March 2026 200-day threshold and 5 with the March 2027 100-day limit, while only 8 have reached readiness for the March 2029 47-day maximum with a median use period of 67 days. This readiness challenge exists against a regulatory surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations, 76% of which are mandatory requirements spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF standards. Zero new ballots have passed since 2022 even as the existing obligation count continues to expand through root program policy updates and audit criteria revisions.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has declined sharply from 2019 levels, when Chrome commented on 67.8% of incidents and Mozilla on 78.0%, to 2025 rates of 18.4% and 9.9% respectively. Apple's participation sits at 5.4% while Microsoft provides 0.0% substantive engagement across 223 total incidents in the latest full year. Chrome has participated in 730 oversight bugs with 293 substantive comments including 112 recent interventions, Mozilla in 818 bugs with 249 substantive comments and 47 recent, and Apple in 46 bugs with 6 substantive comments, all recent, from a corpus of 1,853 total incidents tracked in public bug systems.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 member organizations, but only 21 contribute actively while 35 have zero participation in ballot development or endorsement. Sectigo leads organizational engagement, while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, demonstrating concentrated leadership within an otherwise silent majority. This participation gap means a small subset of the 89 trusted CAs shapes the baseline requirements and audit criteria that all must follow.
intros.audit: Audit letters report a 32% in-period detection rate, meaning auditors identified 132 of the 414 incidents that occurred during periods their audits covered, while the remaining 282 were discovered through other channels. Of 80 parsed audit letters across 83 CAs, 39 show high transparency gaps between audit period end and public disclosure, 4 contain qualified opinions, and 11 CAs changed auditors in 2025. WebTrust self-reporting sits at 59.2% and ETSI at 66.4%, while 9 CAs have adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5, indicating audit letter quality and timing varies substantially across the ecosystem even as clean opinions coexist with real operational incidents discovered post-audit.
